The U.K. and the E.U. have struck a deal to ease some of the trade and travel barriers
that went up when the U.K. left the E.U. in 2020.
As Villa Marx reports, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it a good day for Britain.
This latest deal does away with most border checks on British food sold into the European
Union, something U.K. exporters have complained about since Brexit was finalized six years
ago.
In exchange, Britain will be forced to follow some E.U. rules on agricultural production.
Also, up to 100,000 young Brits will be able to live, work and study in the E.U. for up
to three years and vice versa.
But the E.U. wants British universities to charge European students less money and has
given Britain six months to agree, insisting the deal depends on it.
The Brexit campaigner and now leader of the U.K.'s Reform Party, Nigel Farage, says Prime
Minister Burnham has no democratic mandate to make these changes to the existing Brexit
deal.
For NPR News, I'm Villa Marx in London.
